name: Scott v. Smith (judgment vacated sub nom. Smith v. Scott)
court: Ninth Circuit (from the District of Nevada); judgment vacated and remanded by the Supreme Court of the United States
citation: 109 F.4th 1215 (9th Cir. 2024) (reporter cite as supplied in course materials; not confirmed from the sources read), judgment vacated and remanded sub nom. Smith v. Scott, No. 24-1099 (U.S. Apr. 20, 2026)
decided: July 30, 2024 (Ninth Circuit opinion); judgment vacated April 20, 2026
topic: Prone restraint with bodyweight on a mentally ill man who called 911; restraint asphyxia; qualified immunity under Drummond; Ninth Circuit judgment vacated in light of Zorn v. Linton
summary: Two Las Vegas officers responding to a 911 call from a hallucinating man took him to the ground, rolled him prone, and one applied bodyweight to his back and neck for one to two minutes while his pleas became breathless; he died of what the plaintiffs' expert called restraint asphyxia. The Ninth Circuit affirmed the denial of qualified immunity on the Fourth Amendment claim, holding that Drummond v. City of Anaheim clearly established the violation. On April 20, 2026, the Supreme Court granted certiorari, vacated that judgment, and remanded for further consideration in light of Zorn v. Linton. The Ninth Circuit opinion is no longer good law to cite. The facts remain a teaching case on prone restraint and positional asphyxia.
coverage: The full Ninth Circuit opinion by Judge Desai (with Judge de Alba and District Judge Gutierrez sitting by designation) was read from https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2024/07/30/23-15480.pdf. The slip opinion is headed No. 23-15480, D.C. No. 2:20-cv-01872-RFB-EJY, argued and submitted May 13, 2024, filed July 30, 2024, and marked for publication.
The reporter citation 109 F.4th 1215 was supplied in the assignment. It does not appear in the slip opinion, the Supreme Court order, or Zorn v. Linton, and was not independently confirmed.

The Supreme Court's disposition was read from the April 20, 2026 order list at https://www.supremecourt.gov/orders/courtorders/042026zor_h315.pdf (Order List: 608 U.S.). Under the heading Certiorari, Summary Disposition, No. 24-1099, Smith, Kyle, et al. v. Scott, Rochelle, et al.: the petition for a writ of certiorari is granted, the judgment is vacated, and the case is remanded to the Ninth Circuit for further consideration in light of Zorn v. Linton, 607 U.S. ___ (2026) (per curiam). Justice Sotomayor, Justice Kagan, and Justice Jackson would deny the petition.
Zorn v. Linton was read from the Supreme Court's preliminary print for the companion brief. The order in Smith v. Scott gives no reasoning beyond the reference to Zorn.
No Ninth Circuit decision on remand was located or read. The status of the case after April 20, 2026 is unknown to this brief.

Course materials describe this case as Scott v. Smith as vacated in the restraint line. The brief follows that framing: the facts and the Ninth Circuit's reasoning are described, and the brief states plainly that the Ninth Circuit opinion has been vacated and should not be cited as authority.
facts:
The facts are as the Ninth Circuit stated them on an interlocutory appeal from the denial of qualified immunity, with all disputes resolved in the plaintiffs' favor. Early on March 3, 2019, Roy Scott called 911 and reported multiple assailants outside his Las Vegas apartment with a saw. Dispatch told the responding officers, Kyle Smith and Theodore Huntsman of the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department, that Scott was mentally ill.

Scott was distressed and hallucinating when the officers arrived. After they knocked and identified themselves he yelled for them to break the door down, saying people were inside. The officers heard no one else and did not force entry. They continued knocking and ordering him to the door. Smith told Huntsman the call was a mental health call, and the officers remarked to each other that Scott seemed unstable. Smith called their sergeant, who said they could not do anything without exigent circumstances and suggested they try again to get Scott to the door. About seven minutes after arrival, Scott opened the door.

Smith backed down the stairs. Scott came down holding a metal pipe at his side and dropped it immediately when told to. Disoriented, he twice asked what he was supposed to do. The officers directed him to stand near a wall at the base of the stairs, and he complied. Asked whether he had other weapons, Scott pulled a knife from his pocket, apologized, and handed it to Huntsman handle first without any threatening gesture. Ordered to face the wall under a flashlight, Scott said the light bothered him, that he had paranoid schizophrenia, and that he was paranoid and could not turn around. He twice asked the officers to just put him in the car. Smith told him they were there to help; Scott repeated that he was not fine. The officers later said they concluded he met the criteria for a medical hold.

Smith and Huntsman then grabbed Scott's arms. He pleaded with them in a distressed voice as they pulled him to the ground. They first held his arms at his sides while he lay on his back, screaming and struggling for over two minutes. They then rolled him onto his stomach. With Scott prone and his hands restrained behind his back, Huntsman put his bodyweight on Scott's back and neck for about one to two minutes while Smith restrained his legs. Scott's pleas became increasingly incoherent and breathless. After handcuffing him the officers tried to roll him onto his side; his face was bloody from the ground. Within a few minutes he stopped moving and did not respond to attempts to revive him. He was pronounced dead after paramedics removed him. The plaintiffs' expert found that he died from restraint asphyxia.

Scott's daughter Rochelle and a co administrator of his estate sued the officers and the department under 42 U.S.C. section 1983 for excessive force under the Fourth Amendment and for interference with familial association under the Fourteenth Amendment. The district court denied qualified immunity on both claims, finding genuine disputes about whether Scott reached for his pocket, whether he was taken down or fell, how long he was prone, how long Huntsman's knee was on his back and neck, when he was handcuffed, and the cause of death. The officers appealed.
holding:
What the Ninth Circuit held (July 30, 2024). Affirmed in part and reversed in part. The panel held that, construing the facts in the plaintiffs' favor, the officers violated Scott's Fourth Amendment rights and that the law was clearly established, so qualified immunity was properly denied on that claim. It held that the officers violated Rochelle Scott's Fourteenth Amendment right to familial association but that this right was not clearly established, so they were entitled to qualified immunity on that claim.

On the type of force, the panel held that bodyweight compression on the back and neck of a prone man for one to two minutes while his pleas became breathless, followed by his death, was severe, deadly force, relying on Drummond v. City of Anaheim for the proposition that bodyweight compression on a prone individual can cause compression asphyxia. On the government's interest, the panel found it limited: Scott was not suspected of a crime, had called 911 himself, was known to be mentally ill, relinquished both the pipe and the knife immediately, stood where directed, and made no threatening movements; his resistance after being taken to the ground was screaming and pulling away, not attacking; and the plaintiffs' expert identified less intrusive alternatives, including verbal de escalation, waiting for additional officers for a team takedown, or waiting for EMS for a soft restraint. The panel noted the Ninth Circuit rule that officers need not use the least intrusive means but that failure to consider clear, reasonable, and less intrusive alternatives militates against reasonableness. Balancing, the panel held a reasonable jury could find the force constitutionally excessive and said there were genuine issues whether any force was necessary.

On clearly established law, the panel held that Drummond clearly established that it is unconstitutional to use bodyweight force on the back and neck of a prone and unarmed individual, especially one known to be mentally ill and not suspected of a crime. It rejected the argument that Drummond applies only to an already handcuffed person, reasoning that Scott's hands were restrained behind his back, the functional equivalent, and that Drummond spoke more generally about bodyweight force on a prone individual. It cited its own unpublished decisions applying Drummond despite variations in the facts and distinguished Perez v. City of Fresno, where officers acted at a paramedic's direction.

On the Fourteenth Amendment claim, the panel held that the officers had time to deliberate, because seven minutes passed before any physical contact, they consulted their sergeant, and Scott moved slowly and complied, so the deliberate indifference standard applied, and a jury could find deliberate indifference. But no analogous case clearly established that right, so the officers received qualified immunity on it.

What the Supreme Court did (April 20, 2026). The Court granted the officers' petition for certiorari, vacated the Ninth Circuit's judgment, and remanded for further consideration in light of Zorn v. Linton, the per curiam decision of March 23, 2026 holding that a court must identify a case where an officer acting under similar circumstances was held to have violated the Constitution, with a high degree of specificity, before denying qualified immunity. Justices Sotomayor, Kagan, and Jackson would have denied the petition. The order gives no other reasoning. It does not state that the officers' force was reasonable, does not hold that they are entitled to qualified immunity, and does not mention Drummond.

The effect. The Ninth Circuit's judgment no longer exists. Its opinion is vacated and is not good law to cite, and the clearly established analysis it performed must be redone under Zorn's specificity requirement. Whatever the Ninth Circuit decides on remand will be the operative ruling.
notDecided:
The Supreme Court did not decide whether the officers used excessive force, whether Drummond clearly established the violation, or whether the officers are entitled to qualified immunity. A grant, vacate, and remand order directs the lower court to reconsider; it is not a merits ruling.

The Ninth Circuit itself did not decide that the officers used excessive force. It held that a jury could so find on the plaintiffs' version of disputed facts. No jury has decided those disputes, so far as this brief could confirm.

The Ninth Circuit did not decide the actual cause of death. The cause of death was among the disputed facts the district court identified; the panel accepted the plaintiffs' expert's restraint asphyxia finding only for purposes of the appeal.

The Ninth Circuit did not hold that any prone restraint is unconstitutional. Its analysis turned on bodyweight on the back and neck of a prone, restrained, mentally ill man who was not suspected of a crime and presented no threat.

Nothing in either court's ruling addresses the department's liability, which was not part of the appeal.
inPractice:
Two things must be kept separate: the law and the lesson.

The law. The Ninth Circuit's opinion has been vacated. An officer, instructor, or agency should not cite Scott v. Smith as authority for anything. The Supreme Court sent the case back for the Ninth Circuit to reconsider under Zorn v. Linton, which requires a prior case with similar circumstances, defined with a high degree of specificity, before qualified immunity can be denied. The Supreme Court did not say the officers acted reasonably, did not say Drummond is wrong, and did not grant the officers immunity; it said the Ninth Circuit must look again. Until the Ninth Circuit rules on remand, the state of the law on this specific fact pattern is unsettled, and the controlling Ninth Circuit authority on prone bodyweight restraint remains Drummond and the cases that have applied it.

The lesson. The facts did not change when the judgment was vacated. A man who called for help, disclosed his diagnosis, surrendered two weapons handle first, stood where he was told, and asked to be put in the car was taken to the ground, rolled prone, and compressed on the back and neck until his pleas became breathless and he stopped moving. Dr. Sowards teaches this case in the restraint line with Drummond, Tatum, Spencer v. Pew, Lombardo, and Alves because the mechanism of harm is the same in each: weight on the torso of a prone person, continued after resistance has stopped or was never dangerous, and no monitoring of breathing. Qualified immunity is a defense to damages for the individual officer; it does not prevent a death, a wrongful death verdict against an agency under state law, a policy violation, or a prosecution.

The practical rules are the ones every restraint case teaches: get the person off the stomach as soon as control is achieved, keep weight off the back and neck, treat statements that the person cannot breathe or incoherent and fading sounds as medical emergencies, and when the person is a mentally ill non criminal subject who is complying, ask whether hands on force is needed at all.
trainIt:
Teach this case as a vacated opinion. Begin by telling students the procedural status: the Ninth Circuit denied qualified immunity, the Supreme Court vacated that judgment on April 20, 2026 in light of Zorn v. Linton, and the Ninth Circuit opinion is not to be cited. Then explain why the scenario is still taught: the restraint and the outcome are the training problem regardless of how the immunity question is finally resolved.

Run the encounter as a decision drill with the mental health facts on the table. Dispatch says mentally ill. The man surrenders a pipe and a knife on request. He discloses paranoid schizophrenia, says the light bothers him, says he cannot turn around, and asks to be put in the car. Ask students what the objective is (a medical hold), what the threat is, what resources are available (the sergeant was already on the phone, additional officers and EMS could have been requested), and what the Ninth Circuit panel listed as alternatives the plaintiffs' expert identified: verbal de escalation, a team takedown with more officers, or a soft restraint with EMS. The Ninth Circuit rule, which Barnes v. Felix and Scott v. Henrich both support, is that officers need not choose the least intrusive option, but courts in the Ninth Circuit have said a failure to consider clear and reasonable alternatives weighs against reasonableness.

Teach the restraint mechanics with the clock. On the back for two minutes while struggling; rolled prone; weight on the back and neck for one to two minutes; pleas becoming incoherent and breathless; then unresponsive. Students should learn to recognize the transition from resistance to distress, to move the person to a side or seated recovery position as soon as the hands are secured, and to begin medical assessment at the first sign of breathing difficulty.

Teach Zorn alongside. The Supreme Court's instruction on remand was about specificity of precedent. Students should understand that the question on remand is whether Drummond's facts are close enough to these, not whether prone compression is safe.
caution: This brief covers a vacated opinion. The Ninth Circuit's judgment of July 30, 2024 was vacated by the Supreme Court on April 20, 2026 and the case was remanded for further consideration in light of Zorn v. Linton. The Ninth Circuit opinion is no longer good law and should not be cited as authority. The Supreme Court's order contains no reasoning other than the reference to Zorn and does not decide the merits or the immunity question. No decision on remand was located. The reporter citation 109 F.4th 1215 was not confirmed from a primary source. The facts are the plaintiffs' version as recited on an interlocutory appeal; no court has found that the officers used excessive force or caused Scott's death.

applications.title: Do not cite the Ninth Circuit opinion
applications.body: The Supreme Court vacated the judgment on April 20, 2026 and remanded in light of Zorn v. Linton. A vacated opinion is not authority. Watch for the Ninth Circuit's decision on remand; until then the controlling case on prone bodyweight restraint in the Ninth Circuit remains Drummond.

applications.title: A GVR is not a merits ruling
applications.body: The Supreme Court did not hold that the force was reasonable or that the officers have qualified immunity. It directed the Ninth Circuit to reconsider the clearly established prong under Zorn's specificity requirement. Three Justices would have left the Ninth Circuit's ruling in place.

applications.title: The facts still teach prone restraint
applications.body: On the plaintiffs' version, bodyweight on the back and neck of a prone, restrained, mentally ill man who had surrendered his weapons and complied was followed by breathless pleas, unresponsiveness, and death. The restraint lesson does not depend on the outcome of the immunity question.

applications.title: The hands were secured; the weight stayed on
applications.body: The Ninth Circuit treated hands restrained behind the back as the functional equivalent of handcuffs for Drummond purposes. Whatever the courts decide about immunity, the training rule is to remove weight from the torso as soon as control is achieved and to move the person off the stomach.

applications.title: Immunity is not the only exposure
applications.body: Qualified immunity is a defense to personal damages liability under federal law. It does not resolve state law wrongful death claims, agency policy findings, or the question of whether the restraint was medically safe.

quiz.q: What is the current status of the Ninth Circuit's opinion in Scott v. Smith?
options: It is binding precedent in the Ninth Circuit
It was affirmed by the Supreme Court
Its judgment was vacated by the Supreme Court on April 20, 2026 and remanded for further consideration in light of Zorn v. Linton, so it is not good law to cite
It was reversed on the merits with instructions to grant qualified immunity
quiz.teach: The Supreme Court granted certiorari, vacated, and remanded. The order gives no reasoning beyond the reference to Zorn and does not decide whether the officers are entitled to qualified immunity.

quiz.q: On the plaintiffs' version of the facts, what force did the Ninth Circuit characterize as deadly force?
options: Bodyweight compression on the back and neck of a prone, restrained man for one to two minutes while his pleas became breathless
Shining a flashlight in his face
quiz.teach: The panel relied on Drummond for the proposition that bodyweight compression on a prone individual can cause compression asphyxia and treated the force as severe, deadly force in light of Scott's death.

quiz.q: What did the Supreme Court's April 20, 2026 order in Smith v. Scott decide about the merits?
options: That the officers used reasonable force
Nothing; it vacated the judgment and directed the Ninth Circuit to reconsider in light of Zorn v. Linton
quiz.teach: A grant, vacate, and remand order is not a ruling on the merits. The Ninth Circuit must redo its clearly established analysis under Zorn's requirement of a prior case with similar circumstances defined with specificity.
